newsitem.title: USA: Senators ask more USDA flexibility on CRP rules.
newsitem.headline: Senators ask more USDA flexibility on CRP rules.

text.p: U.S. senators have asked the USDA for more lenient rules Tuesday to ease the predicament of farmers who offered land for the Conservation Reserve but don't know if it was accepted.
The problem was most acute for farmers who need to begin field preparation now for winter wheat in case their bids are rejected. Several million acres could be involved.

Senate Agriculture Committee chairman Richard Lugar, Indiana Republican, was expected to sign the letter to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman. Lugar would prefer an administrative remedy for the problem.

A spokeswoman for Senator Pat Roberts, Kansas Republican, said the letter was a way to defuse the situation. Last week, despite Glickman's strong opposition, the House passed a bill allowing farmers with fall-planted crops to unilaterally extend their Conservation Reserve Program contracts for one year.
"It was made very clear by Secretary Glickman that he would recommend a veto," the aide said. "It (the letter) gives farmers certainty as to what their situation would be."
In the letter, senators asked for rules to allow farmers to do field preparation on expiring CRP acreage without any reduction in the CRP rental payment.
"Specifically, we request that producers be permitted to remove cover crops without penalty immediately," they wrote.
"Producers' need to remove cover is critical regardless of whether they plan to return CRP land to production or intend to improve cover as part of a new contract."

The letter also said senators would oppose any cap, like the 14 million-acre limit pending in the House, on CRP enrollments this year and did not support a Clinton administration proposal to defer some enrollments to offset the cost of stopping a gold mine near Yellowstone National Park. The letter was circulated Wednesday for signature and was to be sent late in the day.
Risk of a veto led to a general agreement, one Senate staff worker said, to keep the CRP extension language off of an emergency spending bill being debated in the Senate.
CRP contracts expire on 21 million acres this fall. Farmers submitted offers to enroll 25.6 million acres. Glickman says USDA will farmers by late May if bids were accepted.

House Agriculture Committee chairman Bob Smith, Oregon Republican, authored the extension bill farmers would be notified too late to plant a crop. Farmers could lose $600 million if deprived of time to plant, he said.
On April 29, the day the extension bill passed, Glickman said growers had several options for land preparation:
--"Early out" termination of contracts on 60-day notice.
--From May 1, farmers in arid areas can destroy cover crop with loss of no more than two months' CRP rental payments.
--From July 1, farmers can begin field preparations with no reduction in payments.
--USDA "will again allow some planting to begin without contract payment reductions" if September sowing is standard.
Cost-share payments were available for reseeding cover if a bid was accepted, Glickman said. Destroying cover crops would not prejudice consideration of an offer.
